The freshwater pearl mussel Pseudunio auricularius exhibits a life history profoundly shaped by its parasitic larval stage and long-term residency in stable riverine habitats. Following external fertilisation and subsequent embryo development within the female's gill chambers, the released glochidia larvae must briefly parasitise a suitable fish host before settling. Upon completing metamorphosis and detaching from the host, the recently metamorphosed juveniles establish themselves in the interstitial spaces of coarse riverbed substrates. At the moment of larval settlement onto the substratum, the shell length of the glochidium is a mere 0.02 centimeters , a size that reflects the lecithotrophic, non-feeding stage of the parasite. Similarly, the shell length at birth for the newly released glochidia, prior to their parasitic phase, is also recorded at 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters]. This diminutive initial dimension necessitates a period of rapid growth and development once the juvenile bivalve begins its benthic existence, filtering organic particulates from the interstitial water column.

As the post-metamorphic juvenile of Pseudunio auricularius grows, its gradual migration into deeper interstitial zones correlates with a slow but consistent increase in shell dimensions. Field surveys of this species across its fragmented range have provided robust estimates for key life-history transitions. The shell length at puberty, representing the point at which gametogenesis is first initiated, has been determined to be 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters]. Achieving this size typically requires many years of benthic accumulation of somatic tissue, a period during which the mollusc faces significant energetic demands from both maintenance and growth. Upon reaching adulthood, the species is capable of attaining a notably large maximum size. The ultimate shell length, observed in the oldest and largest individuals from stable populations, has been measured at 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters]. This substantial maximum dimension is accompanied by a correspondingly considerable adult body mass; the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown Pseudunio auricularius is approximately 210 grams [Wwi = approximately 210 grams], a value derived from size-corrected allometric relationships observed in related unionid species.

Reproductive output in Pseudunio auricularius is constrained by both its slow growth and the necessity of host fish availability. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a single female can release an estimated 8 million glochidia annually [Ri = 8 million glochidia annually]. This massive annual fecundity is a characteristic strategy among freshwater mussels, compensating for the extremely high mortality rates faced by the free-swimming larval stage before it successfully attaches to a host fish. The release of these glochidia is meticulously timed to coincide with the presence of suitable host fish, thereby maximising the probability of successful parasitism and subsequent metamorphosis into the free-living juvenile stage.

The duration of the early developmental phases is strongly modulated by ambient temperature, with cooler conditions extending the incubation period. For the embryonic stages of Pseudunio auricularius, the age at birth, defined as the period from fertilisation to the release of mature glochidia, has been documented as 10 days [ab = 10 days] when the water temperature is maintained at a stable 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This relatively short intra-marsupial development allows females to produce multiple broods within a single favourable spawning season, an adaptation to unpredictable host fish availability. The time elapsed from birth to first successful reproduction, representing the onset of spawning activity, occurs at approximately 8 years after birth [tR = approximately 8 years after birth]. In contrast, the overall life span of this species is exceptionally long, a common trait among large freshwater bivalves. The maximum recorded longevity, or lifespan, for Pseudunio auricularius in its natural environment has been estimated at 70 years [am = 70 years] when measured at a standard temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This extreme longevity reflects a low metabolic rate, a robust shell that deters most predators, and a slow, steady investment in somatic growth and maintenance over many decades.

The extended development and extreme longevity of Pseudunio auricularius position it as a long-term integrator of environmental conditions within its riverine ecosystem. The species' reliance on a host fish for larval metamorphosis creates a particular vulnerability; alterations to fish community structure directly impact recruitment success and population stability. Sexual maturity is attained at a shell length of 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters], which corresponds to an age at puberty of approximately 8 years after birth [tp = approximately 8 years after birth]. The growth rate of the adult bivalve is also quite slow, with annual increments becoming progressively smaller as the individual approaches its asymptotic size of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters]. Weaning, defined as the completion of the parasitic larval phase and the transition to independent benthic feeding, occurs at approximately 10 days after hatching [tx = approximately 10 days after hatching]. Conservation efforts for Pseudunio auricularius, therefore, must focus not only on maintaining water quality and substrate stability for the adult mussels but also on ensuring the persistence of healthy, migratory host fish populations to support the parasitic glochidial stage and complete the species' complex life cycle.
